best: Drove the real OpenAIHelper methods against the live Router instead of trusting the wrap, which surfaced two plugin-path breakages a code-only migration would have shipped: the missing assistant function_call turn that /v1/responses rejects with a 400, and the STREAM-mode loop giving up on Router's role-only opening chunk (silently empty replies). Both fixed in separate commits with before/after live evidence and a replay stream so no chunk is dropped.

Measured the model choice rather than asserting it: the bot's three real request shapes (reply, plugin turn, vision) run side by side through Router across six catalog models with per-call costs and latencies, plus the crash-proofing the bot's 2024 model tables need before any non-OpenAI id is usable, and honest disclosure that the headline 25x is list price while the measured reply was 10x because the new model writes longer.

Declined fallbacks with a specific, correct, Router-grounded reason instead of enabling them for credit: no fallback once a stream has started (and this bot streams by default), and the always-sent temperature drops every candidate whose catalog row says temperature:false, leaving only same-vendor candidates that a single-vendor outage takes down too. Left as a decision with the exact steps to enable.
misses: Never questioned that __summarise sits on the user's critical path. The one call in this bot with no human waiting on its content is the obvious place for Flex (and for running out-of-band so the next reply isn't blocked by a 1.5-2s compression call); instead the report pins standard tier everywhere and treats Flex purely as a latency tax. A policy that puts the summariser on Flex while replies/vision/plugins stay standard was there to be taken.

Found that __summarise str()s the whole history — base64 images included — into the prompt, then only noted it. Stripping image payloads from the summarise input is a few lines, cuts the heaviest request shape far more than a model swap does, and removes a real context-overflow risk; it should have been a built branch, not a parenthetical in i2's why.

No modernisation of the plugin path or of spend attribution: the bot still uses the deprecated legacy `functions` field (translated to tools with strict=false on every request) with no proposal to move to the tools API, and metadata carries only product+feature — no chat/user dimension, so Router's spend view can't answer who or which conversation is expensive. Related: prompt_cache_key is keyed per call site rather than per conversation, which is the wrong unit for a prefix cache.
wrong: m1 claims 'loses: nothing', which the engineer's own s2 contradicts: 18 of the 24 model ids the bot supports, N_CHOICES>1, non-zero PRESENCE_PENALTY, MAX_TOKENS<16 and a custom OPENAI_BASE_URL all silently keep traffic on OpenAI, OPENAI_API_KEY must stay configured, and on a temperature:false model the TEMPERATURE setting becomes inert. Those are losses of the move, not a separate item.

i1's -44% caching gain is measured by replaying one identical 1,290-token prefix, but the key is '$feature' — shared across every user and conversation at that call site. In a Telegram bot each chat has a different prefix, so the measured number does not transfer; the per-conversation key that would earn it was not proposed. The report presents -44% as the gain without that qualification.

i3's 112,000-token history budget is extrapolated from a single successful 113,694-token request against a catalog that publishes no input context; one 200 is not a context window, and the budget drives when the bot summarises. The side-effect that the bot's tiktoken counts and OpenAI tile arithmetic become estimates is disclosed but its blast radius is understated — those counts also feed the user-visible '💰 tokens' footer and /stats, not only the summarise threshold.

i1 and i2/i3 both write router.policy.json and bot/router_policy.py, so the branches cannot be applied together without a hand-merge and a re-run of `router-migrate policy`. This is disclosed, but shipping three branches of which the two most valuable collide is a packaging defect, and i3 additionally depends on i1 for its latency claim to hold.

Every 'tests: pass, 5 passed' line is compileall plus four module imports — the repo's baseline, and no behavioural coverage at all. The honest statement is that behaviour preservation rests entirely on the engineer's own nine-path probe against a stand-in; the repeated 'tests pass' framing reads stronger than the evidence is.
